overview:
Tanzania occupies a great slab of East Africa between the Indian Ocean and three of Africa's largest lakes. It is about twice the size of California and holds both the continent's highest point, Mount Kilimanjaro, and a share of Lake Tanganyika, the second deepest lake on Earth. The spice island of Zanzibar lies off the coast, Dar es Salaam is the biggest city and main port, and Dodoma, inland at the country's center, is the official capital.

About 65 million people live in Tanzania, in more than 120 ethnic groups. Swahili is the national language, spoken by nearly everyone and taught in primary schools, with English used in government and universities; that shared language has helped keep the country unusually united. Tanzania is a republic. Most people farm, growing maize, cassava, coffee and cloves, while visitors come for national parks and reserves that cover roughly a third of the land, among the largest protected areas anywhere.
landAndNature: Mount Kilimanjaro rises alone out of the plains to 5,895 meters, the highest mountain in Africa and the tallest freestanding mountain on Earth, carrying glaciers almost on the equator. The Serengeti's grasslands carry the largest land migration in the world, roughly two million wildebeest, zebra and gazelle circling year after year in search of rain. Ngorongoro Crater, a collapsed volcano 20 kilometers across, holds a whole ecosystem inside its walls. The Great Rift Valley splits the country and cradles Lake Tanganyika, alive with hundreds of fish species found nowhere else. Coral reefs and mangroves line the coast, and chimpanzees live in the forests at Gombe.
peopleAndCulture: Ugali, a stiff maize porridge, is eaten with beans, greens or grilled fish, while the coast and Zanzibar add coconut, cloves, cardamom and cinnamon to rice and seafood; Zanzibar's night market grills skewers by lamplight. Taarab music blends Swahili poetry with Arab and Indian instruments, and bongo flava is the pop sound of the cities. The Maasai herd cattle across the northern plains in red cloaks, and the Hadza near Lake Eyasi are among the last hunter-gatherer communities in Africa. Soccer is followed passionately. Greetings are long and unhurried, a matter of good manners, and Swahili proverbs season everyday speech.
history: Some of the oldest known human footprints, made about 3.6 million years ago, were preserved in volcanic ash at Laetoli, and nearby Olduvai Gorge has yielded famous fossils of early humans. Swahili city-states such as Kilwa grew wealthy on Indian Ocean trade from the 900s. Portugal and later the sultans of Oman controlled Zanzibar, which became a center of the clove and slave trades. Germany colonized the mainland in the 1880s, and Britain took over after World War I. Tanganyika became independent in 1961 under Julius Nyerere and united with Zanzibar in 1964 to form Tanzania. Nyerere promoted Swahili and a village socialism called ujamaa; multiparty elections returned in 1995.
funFacts: Kilimanjaro is the tallest freestanding mountain in the world, and climbers pass through five climate zones on the way up.
Tanzanite, a blue-violet gemstone, is found in only one place on Earth, a few square kilometers near Kilimanjaro.
Footprints preserved in volcanic ash at Laetoli show human ancestors walking upright about 3.6 million years ago.
Tanzania sets aside roughly a third of its territory as parks and reserves, one of the largest shares of any country.
Zanzibar's clove trees once supplied much of the world, and the scent of drying spices still hangs over its villages.
